The primary objective of the Institutional Repository for Information Sharing (IRIS) is to provide free digital access t o the scientific and technical publications of the World Health Organization (WHO), including contributions from its Country Offices, Regional Offices, and Headquarters. Additionally, IRIS encompasses the mandates established by the Organization’s Governing Bodies in collaboration with its Member States.

How health law contributes to achieving universal health coverage
World Health Organization (Publication Date: 2026-11-04, Accepted: 2026-11-04, Available Online: 2026-11-04)
Show more
This publication examines how legal frameworks contribute to the achievement and sustainability of universal health coverage (UHC). As part of the UHC Law in Practice series, it provides a conceptual framework for understanding the role of law in translating political commitments into enforceable rights, institutional responsibilities, governance arrangements, and accountability mechanisms that support equitable access to quality health services without financial hardship. The document describes ten interrelated legal dimensions of UHC, including access rights, financing, benefit packages, workforce and medicines, quality regulation, governance, equity, private sector engagement, and progressive realization, while also addressing emerging legal issues related to digital health, data governance, and artificial intelligence.

Drawing on comparative examples from countries including Brazil, Colombia, France, Ghana, India, the Netherlands, Rwanda, South Africa, Thailand and the United Kingdom, the publication illustrates how different legal approaches influence the design, implementation and resilience of health systems. It identifies common legal principles and governance mechanisms that support universality, equity, financial protection and accountability, providing a practical reference for policymakers, legal practitioners and health system stakeholders seeking to strengthen UHC through effective legal and regulatory frameworks.

Fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh meetings of the WHO Technical Advisory Group on candidate vaccine prioritization (TAG-CVP) for Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak response: meetings report, 1 September, 19 October, 22 October and 2 November 2026
World Health Organization (Publication Date: 2026-11-04, Accepted: 2026-11-04, Available Online: 2026-11-04)
Show more
This meeting report summarizes the deliberations and recommendations of the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritization (TAG–CVP) following four meetings held between September and November 2026 in response to the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May 2026. The Group reviewed evidence on two Bundibugyo virus-specific vaccine candidates, ChAdOx1 BDBV (University of Oxford) and mRNA-1469 (Moderna), to assess their suitability for clinical evaluation and outbreak response.

The review covered preclinical toxicology, animal challenge studies, interim phase 1 safety and immunogenicity results, and vaccine manufacturing and availability. Both candidates demonstrated protection in ferret and non-human primate studies, induced antibody responses within 14 days and showed acceptable reactogenicity profiles in preliminary clinical trials. The Group also considered uncertainties concerning rare serious adverse events associated with the respective vaccine platforms. Based on the available safety, immunogenicity and protection data, TAG–CVP unanimously recommended including both candidates in the ongoing phase 2/3 clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

WHO estimates of the global burden of foodborne diseases 2000-2021: key findings
World Health Organization (Publication Date: 2026-11-04, Accepted: 2026-11-04, Available Online: 2026-11-04)
Show more
This key findings report presents updated World Health Organization (WHO) estimates of the global burden of foodborne diseases for 2000–2021, covering 42 biological and chemical hazards across 194 WHO Member States. In 2021, foodborne diseases caused an estimated 866 million illnesses, 1.52 million deaths and 57.1 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) worldwide. Diarrhoeal diseases accounted for most illnesses, while noncommunicable diseases associated with chemical hazards caused the majority of deaths and DALYs. Children under five experienced a disproportionate burden, particularly from diarrhoeal diseases, and substantial regional disparities persisted despite declining disease burden rates over the study period.

The 2026 edition expands the range of hazards assessed and incorporates updated systematic reviews, structured expert judgement and hierarchical imputation modelling. It examines geographical and age-related differences, foodborne transmission pathways and associated productivity losses. The updated estimates provide an evidence base for strengthening food safety policies, prioritizing preventive interventions and monitoring progress in reducing the global burden of foodborne diseases.
